To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

2D‐2D registration can be used to determine the 3D position of a patient with a precision of 0.5mm and 0.2 degrees, and that 2D registration can determine 3D rotations with a precision of up to 0.4 degrees.
3D registration of EPIDimages with MDRRs is feasible and can be used to determine patient setup with a precision of 0.5‐0.7 mm and 0.2‐0.4°.

the 3D position and orientation of a patient in external beam radiotherapypre‐treatment can be determined using only two orthogonal projection images, and that this method has a precision better than 1 mm and 1°.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a 2‐D/3‐D registration method for external beam radiotherapy, which is capable of determining 3D rotations and/or translations of a patient with respect to a treatment machine with a precision better than 0,5mm and 0,5° respectively.
a method that can be used for 3D patient localization and verification in external beam radiotherapeutic treatments.
the development of a method to register EPIDimages to digitally reconstructed radiographs (MDRR) for the determination of patient setup in external beam radiotherapeutic procedures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

a 2D/3D registration method can be implemented for external beam radiotherapy with a high precision and accuracy, but that the method requires further investigation of the influence of the various parameters on registration precision.
the method is robust for the registration of 2D‐images and 3D patient positions in external beam radiotherapies.
3D‐3D image registration is not required for 2D‐2D EPID‐MDRR registration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the registration method is robust and accurate, but that the precision of the registration depends on the complexity of the object and the projection images.
the 2D‐2D method is not sufficient and that the 2‐D‐3D method is a promising method for patient setup verification.
3D patient pose in radiation therapy can be determined with a precision of 1 mm and 1°, provided that image preprocessing is applied.
The main takeaway from our work is that
3D‐2D image‐based registration is a powerful technique that can be used for patient position verification and for patient setup correction.
the registration of 3D rotations and 3D translations is possible with an accuracy better than 0,5mm/0,2°.
the 2D‐to‐3D registration problem is not as difficult as it may seem, and that it can be solved with a high degree of precision.
